Lessons.Title: Reasoning about Exponential Graphs (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: investigate effect of multiplier b and coefficient a on graphs of a·b^x, comparing initial values, growth/decay direction and steepness using multiple equations on common axes. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 12, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/12/preparation.html and student lesson https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/12/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The publisher encourages dynamic graphing technology; text calculations are not proof that a device was used.

Original comparative functions on x≥0: F(x)=50(1.5)^x, G(x)=50(2)^x and H(x)=50(.75)^x. All share vertical intercept (0,50). At x1 their values are75,100,37.5; at x2 they are112.5,200,28.125. F and G grow while H decays. Over positive x, larger growth factor creates faster increase from the same starting value.

Changing initial coefficient instead of multiplier moves intercept: J(x)=80(1.5)^x starts80 but grows at same 50%-per-period rate as F. If a is negative the sign and graph relation differ, but these practice examples intentionally use positive a to isolate factor effects.

Student task: draw or use actual authorized graphing technology to compare F,G,H, label intersecting t0, explain why G outpaces F for positive x, and describe changes with coefficient a while holding b fixed. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for table, graph comparison, parameter interpretation and clear differentiation between multiplier and additive slope.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common initial value
KeyConcepts.Definition: Functions with the same a in a·b^x share output a at x=0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Growth versus decay
KeyConcepts.Definition: b>1 gives increase for positive a;0<b<1 gives decrease.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check factor without confusing it with percent change.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parameter a scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Changing a scales outputs while preserving factor b.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare all three at x1
WorkedExamples.Question: Find F1,G1,H1.
WorkedExamples.Method: Derive the specific first-party mathematical rule, independently verify it and interpret with the stated domains.
Steps: All began at50 but b changes direction/rate.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each output is initial50 times respective factor.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare x2 growth or decay
WorkedExamples.Question: Find F2,G2,H2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Derive the specific first-party mathematical rule, independently verify it and interpret with the stated domains.
Steps: F and G increase, H decreases.
WorkedExamples.Check: All x2 values equal two successive multiplications.

WorkedExamples.Title: Change initial value separately
WorkedExamples.Question: J(x)=80(1.5)^x. Find J0 and J2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Derive the specific first-party mathematical rule, independently verify it and interpret with the stated domains.
Steps: Relative multiplier over one period is1.5, same as F.
The intercept changed, not growth factor.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming same initial value means same graph
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different b produces different outputs for x≠0.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Interpreting factor1.5 as an increase of1.5 units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It is50% of current value per step.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming an interactive plot was operated from a written sketch
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The file contains only static examples.

SummaryPoints: Coefficient a sets initial output, factor b controls repeated scaling.
With a50, factors1.5,2 and.75 give distinct graphs.
Model comparisons require common axes and appropriate domains.
Teacher reviews graphs, interpretations and genuine technology evidence.
